name: Alejandro Jodorowsky
milestone_by_age_26: Founded the 50-member Teatro Mimico in Santiago at age 18 and joined Marcel Marceau's mime troupe in Paris by age 24, writing notable routines including 'The Cage' and 'The Mask Maker.'
early_history_summary: Jodorowsky dropped out of university in Chile and founded his own theater troupe, Teatro Mimico, in 1947 at age 18, growing it to 50 members by 1952. He moved to Paris in 1953 to study mime under Étienne Decroux and joined Marcel Marceau's company, creating several performed routines and touring worldwide.

name: Jean-Luc Godard
milestone_by_age_26: Published first film criticism in La Gazette du cinéma at age 20 and first article in Cahiers du cinéma at age 21; made first short film Opération béton at age 24.
early_history_summary: Godard grew up in a wealthy Franco-Swiss family in Switzerland and moved to Paris around 1949 to study ethnology at the Sorbonne. He became immersed in ciné-club culture, attending the Cinémathèque Française and the Ciné-Club du Quartier Latin, where he met Truffaut, Chabrol, Rohmer, and Rivette. He published his first film articles at age 20 and joined Cahiers du cinéma as a critic at 21.
family_context_summary: Godard was born into a wealthy Franco-Swiss Protestant family. His father was a Swiss physician and his mother was the granddaughter of Julien Monod, a founder of Banque Paribas. The family moved to Switzerland when Godard was four.

evidence_summary: Godard came from a wealthy Franco-Swiss Protestant family; his mother was the granddaughter of a founder of Banque Paribas and his father was a physician. He began attending Paris ciné-clubs around 1949-1950 and published his first film criticism in La Gazette du cinéma at age 20, followed by his first Cahiers du cinéma article at 21. He made his first short film, Opération béton, at age 24. The Cahiers circle—including Truffaut, Rohmer, Rivette, and Chabrol—provided an exceptional peer network, while André Bazin served as a mentor figure. name: Helmut Newton
milestone_by_age_26: Published his first magazine cover photograph in the Australasian in June 1945 at age 25, and established his own photography studio in Melbourne's Flinders Lane in 1946 at age 26.
early_history_summary: Newton was born Helmut Neustädter in Berlin to a Jewish family; his father owned a button factory. Interested in photography from age 12, he apprenticed with photographer Yva from 1936 to 1938. Fleeing Nazi Germany in 1938, he traveled through Singapore before being interned and sent to Australia in 1940. After serving in the Australian Army, he set up his own studio in 1946 and began building a fashion photography career in Melbourne.
family_context_summary: Newton was born to a Jewish family in Berlin. His father Max Neustädter owned a button factory that was lost under the Nuremberg Laws. His parents fled to Argentina; Newton was sent to Australia via Singapore. The family was separated by wartime displacement.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family connection to photography is documented. His father was a button factory owner.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Yva apprenticeship, Jewish refugee, Melbourne studio, fashion photography
evidence_summary: Newton apprenticed with Berlin photographer Yva from age 16 to 18, gaining early technical foundation. Fleeing Nazi persecution as a Jewish refugee, he spent time in Singapore and was interned in Australia before establishing a studio in Melbourne's Flinders Lane in 1946 at age 26. His first magazine cover was published in June 1945. The adversity of displacement and internment shaped his self-reliant approach to building a photography career in a new country. His father's button factory was confiscated under Nazi laws, eliminating any family financial platform.

name: Claude Chabrol
milestone_by_age_26: Became a staff writer for Cahiers du cinéma in 1953 at age 23, co-developing the politique des auteurs, and founded the production company AJYM in 1956 at age 26.
early_history_summary: Chabrol studied pharmacology and literature at the Sorbonne and briefly attended the École Libre des Sciences Politiques in Paris. He became involved in ciné-club culture, frequenting the Cinémathèque Française and the Ciné-Club du Quartier Latin, where he met Rohmer, Rivette, Godard, and Truffaut. After military service, he joined Cahiers du cinéma as a critic in 1953 and co-authored a landmark Hitchcock monograph with Rohmer in 1957.
family_context_summary: Chabrol's family background is not extensively documented in reviewed sources. His education at the Sorbonne and Sciences Po suggests a comfortable middle-class upbringing. He married Agnes Goute in 1952.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cahiers du cinéma, Cinémathèque, Paris film culture, AJYM productions

name: Steve McQueen
milestone_by_age_26: Made his Broadway debut in 1955 at age 25 in 'A Hatful of Rain' and his first film appearance in 'Somebody Up There Likes Me' in 1956 at age 26; accepted into the Actors' Studio from 2,000 applicants.
early_history_summary: McQueen had a turbulent childhood: abandoned by his father, abused by his stepfather, and sent to Boys Republic reform school at 14. After serving in the Marines (1947-1950), he used the GI Bill to study acting at Sanford Meisner's Neighborhood Playhouse in New York starting in 1952. He was one of only five students accepted into Lee Strasberg's Actors' Studio from 2,000 applicants, alongside Martin Landau.
family_context_summary: McQueen was born to a single mother in Beech Grove, Indiana. His father, a stunt pilot, abandoned the family when Steve was six months old. His mother was an alcoholic. He was raised by grandparents and a great-uncle on a farm, then by his mother and abusive stepfather. He was sent to Boys Republic reform school at 14 and joined the Marines at 17.

name: Bruce McLaren

Bruce began racing at 15 in 1952, winning his first hillclimb. He won a 'Driver to Europe' scholarship in 1957, moved to Europe in 1958, made his F1 debut at the 1958 German Grand Prix, and joined the Cooper works team in 1959 alongside Jack Brabham.
family_context_summary: McLaren grew up in Auckland, New Zealand. His father Les McLaren was president of the Auckland Car Club in 1950-51 and actively raced and rebuilt cars, providing Bruce with early immersion in motorsport and engineering. The family workshop in Remuera was where Bruce learned car mechanics.
